segments.english: As for what you wrote, that Ze'ir Anpin is the son of Abba and Imma, and that he is the father of the effects that come after him, and he has a sister, his Nukva; all of it is a parable and an allusion concerning the sefirot. As for what you wrote, that no partzuf is to be worshipped, this is known on the lips of all the Kabbalists, and they have no need of your warning. As for what you wrote in the name of the Rambam, that they are five, those called heretics, etc. Who is the one who says there is no God, or that there are two, or that He has a body, or that He is not alone, the One, or that he worships another in order to be an intercessor, or the one who says he found signs, or the one who says the world was created something from something, God forbid. But a grudge has already risen in your heart, and you read the holy books, take their words at their plain sense, and rely on your understanding. And you forgot what the wisest of the wise said: "and do not lean on your own understanding." Since you have already informed me that you understand, resolve my doubts, which I sent you and which I am about to send. As for what you wrote, that you understood that many and great men of wise heart, early and late, withdraw from it: God forbid that there be any sage who withdraws from it. And if there is one who withdraws from it, he himself admits openly that it is from his lack of knowledge of it. As for what you wrote, as the Ribash and the Chavot Yair wrote, you speak falsehood about them. And they are two valid witnesses to testify against you that you speak lies. And these are the words of the Ribash, in brief: "Rabbi Peretz ha-Kohen did not speak of those sefirot and did not attach importance to them. Also he heard from his mouth that Rabbi Shimshon of Kinon used to say: 'I pray to know this child,' that is, to remove from the hearts of the Kabbalists the idea that they pray at one time to one sefirah and at another time to another sefirah. Also in the Eighteen Benedictions they have, in each and every one, a specific intention toward a known sefirah. And all this is a very strange thing in the eyes of anyone who is not a Kabbalist like them, and they think it is the belief in duality. And he heard one of the would-be philosophers speaking in disparagement of the Kabbalists, and he would say: 'The Christians are believers in the Trinity, and the Kabbalists are believers in the tens.' And he asked the elderly sage Don Yosef ibn Shushan, who was a sage in the Talmud, who had studied philosophy and was a Kabbalist, pious, great, and scrupulous in the commandments. And he said to him: 'How is it that you Kabbalists direct one blessing to one known sefirah and another blessing to another sefirah. Furthermore, are there divinities for the sefirot? That a man should pray to them?' And they answered him: 'God forbid that the prayer be anything but to the Name, may He be blessed, the Cause of causes; but one directs the thought to draw the flow to that sefirah which relates to the thing he asks for, just as you would say that in the blessing for the righteous one should direct to the sefirah called Chesed, which is the attribute of mercy, etc.' And he brought him a parable on this. He answered and said: 'And behold, very good.' And he said: 'I do not commit myself to that wisdom, since I did not receive it from the mouth of a Kabbalist sage.' 'And if I have seen commentaries on the secrets of the Ramban, they reveal a handbreadth and cover handbreadths.' And he said that a certain sage explained the Kabbalah not as the Ramban holds, and therefore he said that the words of that sage shall be his alone. And he ended his words." Therefore I say that one must not rely on such words, except from the mouth of a Kabbalist sage.

tokens.note: Ze'ir Anpin: Aramaic for 'Small Face'; the Hebrew writes the initials ז"א. Ze'ir alone is 'Ze'ir'.
Abba: 'Father', the name of a partzuf.
Imma: 'Mother', the name of a partzuf.
Cause and effect: the author's עלה and עלול. 'Effects' are what a cause produces.
Nukva: 'Female', the feminine partner of the partzuf (his Nukva).
Partzuf: a Kabbalistic entity, kept transliterated (the ordinary sense is 'face').
The Rambam (Maimonides). The list is the one the questioner gives in the Rambam's name.
Heretics (minim).
'Etc.' marks a truncated quotation: the list goes on in the source, and the author does not give it.
Literally 'signs'.
Literally 'something from something' (יש מיש).
God forbid (ח"ו).
Literally 'according to its plain sense'; the Hebrew is in the plural, 'the books' plain sense'.
The verse is quoted in the following words.
Literally 'the wise one of the wise' (חכם החכמים).
Prov 3:5, 'and do not lean on your own understanding'.
Literally 'with a full mouth' (בפה מלא): openly, without reservation.
The Ribash: Rabbi Yitzchak ben Sheshet.
Chavot Yair, the book the abbreviation names; cited by its title.

tokens.gloss: and these are the words of

tokens.note: ר' written in full: Rabbi.
שר' is ש' ('that') with ר' ('Rabbi').
'The child': as written. The text does not explain the phrase.
The Eighteen Benedictions (the Amidah).
'Would-be philosophers' (המתפלספים): a term of disparagement.
The Hebrew writes הנצרים (Notzrim), the term for the Christians.
'The tens': the ten sefirot.
ibn: 'son of'.

tokens.gloss: to the Name, may He be blessed
tokens.note: השי"ת: the Name, may He be blessed.
'Cause of causes' (עלת העלות).
Literally 'lights': commentaries called 'lights' on the Ramban's secrets.
The Ramban (Nachmanides).
An idiom: they reveal a handbreadth and conceal handbreadths, that is, reveal little and hide much.
כד' is כדעת: 'as the view of'.

grammar: This paragraph is the respondent's letter, answering the questioner in the second person. Each point opens with ומה שכתבת ('as for what you wrote') and is answered in turn.
The Ribash passage opens with the formula וז"ל and is given in double quotation marks. The speakers inside it are in single quotation marks.
ואל בינתך אל תשען (Prov 3:5) is a verse quoted as a saying. תשען is the imperfect with אל, a negative command: 'do not lean'.
שאין לעבוד is impersonal: 'one may not worship', rendered 'that no partzuf is to be worshipped'.
היה with the participle (היה אומר) gives a habitual past: 'used to say'.
segments.note: The paragraph is in the respondent's voice. The quotation from the Ribash is given as the writer gives it; the sentence in the Ribash's own voice that closes with וחתם דבריו ends the quotation. 'The Christians' renders הנצרים and 'something from something' renders יש מיש, both by the ruling. The Kabbalists' answer in the story is kept as Don Yosef's account gives it.
apparatus: Base text from Wikisource; the 1931 scan is not yet collated (Q2).
Prov 3:5: 'ואל בינתך אל תשען' ('and do not lean on your own understanding'), quoted as the sage's words.
The text writes הנצרים (Notzrim) for the Christians.
